description: Your leg swing number exposes the tendons buried deep inside your hips. Learn how the iliopsoas and rectus femoris cables store and return energy, the five mistakes making them stiffer, and the daily rhythm drill that turns a choppy swing into a spring.

scenes.narration: Stand tall, one hand on a wall. Lift your right leg and let it swing, front to back, loose like a pendulum. Do not kick it. Do not force it. Just start the swing and let the leg do what it wants. Now count. How many full, smooth swings do you get in THIRTY SECONDS before the swing turns choppy and small? That number is your LEG SWING TEST, and it is not really about flexibility. It is about the tendons buried deep inside your hips. Write the number down. At the end of this video I will tell you exactly what it means, and why the way most guys train their hips is quietly making those tendons worse.

scenes.label: SMOOTH SWINGS IN 30 SECONDS
scenes.narration: Here is the line. TWENTY-FOUR smooth swings in thirty seconds means your hip tendons are storing energy and handing it back, the way springs should. Under fifteen, the swing dies early, and your muscles end up dragging a dead leg around. Over thirty, your hips move with the loose rhythm of a sprinter, and here is the good news: that rhythm is trainable, and it has almost nothing to do with how much muscle you carry.
scenes.sub: under 15: stiff cables - 15 to 24: building - over 30: wired hips

lines: Rectus femoris: two joints, one cable.
beats.title: THE TWO CABLES

scenes.narration: Look at the front of your hip, deep under the surface. Two tendons run the whole show. The ILIOPSOAS tendon, from the deepest hip flexor in your body, anchors to the top of your thigh bone. The RECTUS FEMORIS tendon crosses the hip and the knee, one cable serving two joints. Every step you take, every stair, every sprint stride, these cables load up like springs and hand the energy back for free. That is the part nobody tells skinny guys. A tendon is not a rope that wears out. It is living tissue, and it remodels itself around the loads you give it. Give it rhythm and tension and it grows STIFFER, and stiffness here is a gift. A stiff hip tendon returns energy. A slack one leaks it, and the muscle next door pays the bill. When the swing stays smooth past twenty, the cables are timing the return for you. When it falls apart at ten, your muscles are doing a job the tendons should be sharing. And there is a simple way to feel this yourself. Swing the leg, then stop it suddenly with your hand at the top of the swing. Notice how the leg wants to keep traveling and then settle. That settle is the tendon taking up the load and handing it back. A trained hip settles in one clean motion. An untrained hip wobbles and argues. Your number counts the argument.

lines: in a system that lets go.
beats.title: BRAKES OFF

scenes.narration: But there is a second system hiding inside that swing: your nerves. A smooth pendulum swing is not just strong tendons. It is a muscle that knows how to switch OFF. Every swing forward needs the hip flexors to fire, then release completely so the leg can fall back. When the swing gets choppy, the brakes are staying on. The muscles are guarding, and guarding is a habit, not a weakness. This is why the test counts SMOOTH swings, not fast ones. Forcing speed just teaches the brakes to squeeze harder. Slow, loose, repeatable rhythm teaches the nervous system to let go, and a tendon can only spring in a system that lets it. Researchers who study tendon training keep landing on the same point: the tissue adapts over weeks of steady loading, slower than muscle, which is exactly why rhythm work beats random effort. This is also why the swing is such an honest warm-up. Sixty seconds of loose swinging before you train tells the brakes to stand down, and the whole lower body moves better for it.

Now look at what these cables decide for the rest of your training. Your squat depth is not really about your knees. It is about whether the hip tendons let the thigh travel. Your stride length when you run is set by the same spring. Even the ache some guys feel at the side of the hip comes from a stabilizer tendon, the GLUTE MED tendon, doing a job it was never loaded for. Here is the pattern worth remembering. The hip has cables in front that swing the leg, and cables on the side that keep the pelvis level. Train only one team and the other starts complaining. Your leg swing test reads the front team. The side team shows up later, in your balance and your squat. A complete hip is not a flexible hip. It is a hip where every cable has been given a reason to get strong.

Here is where being light stops being the insult and starts being the edge. A pendulum is easier to swing when it weighs less. Your leg is that pendulum. A lighter leg costs less energy per swing, so in the same thirty seconds you can stack more clean, high-quality reps than the heavy guy whose muscles are burning by swing twelve. Tendons do not count weight lifted. They count LOADING CYCLES, clean tension, again and again. That is your lane. More cycles, better rhythm, faster remodeling. The big guy is swinging a sledgehammer. You are swinging a metronome, and metronomes win this test every single time. This is also why your number can jump fast in the first two weeks. The first gains are not new tissue. They are timing, and timing is free.
Swing with me. One leg at a time, loose and tall, thirty seconds each, two rounds per leg. Let it be a pendulum, never a kick. Go.

Now the five mistakes that are quietly destroying your hip tendons. Mistake one: KICKING for range. Forcing the leg higher with muscle teaches the brakes, not the spring. Mistake two: marathon stretching. Long, aggressive front-hip stretches right before you train leave the tendon temporarily slack, the opposite of a spring. Mistake three: fast band work only. Snappy, light reps never give the tendon the slow, heavy tension it actually remodels from. Mistake four: never loading the hip while it is LENGTHENED, the position where the cable works hardest. Mistake five: training your strong side and skipping the stiff one, so the gap quietly becomes the injury. The fix is boring and it works. Daily loose swings for rhythm. Slow split squats, three seconds down, for tension. And patience measured in weeks, because tendons remodel slower than muscles. One more thing. If the front of your hip pinches, clicks with pain, or aches for more than two weeks, stop and see a professional. That is not weakness. That is information.

scenes.label: RETEST YOUR SWING
scenes.narration: So, your number. Under FIFTEEN: your hip cables are untrained, not broken, and untrained is the most fixable diagnosis in training. Fifteen to twenty-four: the springs are waking up, and rhythm work will move you fast. Over TWENTY-FOUR: your hips are wired, and the swing is free energy. Whatever your number was, it is a starting line, not a verdict on you. Train the swings daily, retest on day thirty, and put today's number in the comments. Just the number. That thread becomes the scoreboard we all check next month.
scenes.sub: same leg, same clock, same rules - compare honestly

scenes.narration: Your legs already know how to swing. Now the cables learn how to spring. Retest in thirty days and bring me the new number. Subscribe, because next time we test the cable that decides whether your knee is a spring or a hinge. This is {channel}. Train the cable.

title: 5 hip tendon training Mistakes That Are Destroying Your hip tendons
